title: Defining Scope and Constraints
description: Learn to establish clear boundaries and identify constraints early in a system design interview to avoid scope creep and misaligned solutions.

data.text: Scope defines the boundaries of your system — what is included, what is excluded, and where you can safely make simplifying assumptions. Without clear scope, your design drifts into irrelevant complexity. Constraints are the hard limits that shape every architectural decision, from budget and timeline to technology choices and regulatory requirements.

In interviews, scope is rarely given upfront. You must define it through strategic questioning. A well-scoped problem is solvable in 30 to 45 minutes. An over-scoped problem leads to superficial coverage of every component, while an under-scoped problem wastes time on trivial details.

data.title: Key Scope Questions:
items: Which user roles are in scope for this iteration?
Are we designing the full system or just a specific component?
Should we include mobile apps, or focus on the backend API?
Do we need to handle legacy systems or integrations?
Is real-time functionality required, or is batch processing acceptable?

data.text: Constraints are non-negotiable limits that narrow your solution space. They can be technical, business, or regulatory in nature. Common constraints include maximum latency requirements, budget caps, compliance rules like GDPR, technology stack restrictions, and team expertise limitations.

rows: Must use AWS, must support offline mode
Shrinks feature set and infrastructure options
Requires encryption, audit logs, data residency

data.title: Avoiding Scope Creep
data.text: Interviewers often expand the scope midway through your design. Politely note the new requirement, confirm it is in scope, and adjust your trade-off analysis rather than redesigning from scratch.

data.caption: Scope boundaries in system design
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Interview Problem] --> B{In Scope?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Design Component]
    B -->|No| D[Assumption / Exclude]
    C --> E[Constraint Check]
    E -->|Pass| F[Proceed]
    E -->|Fail| G[Revise Approach]

data.text: Every design relies on assumptions. In an interview, stating your assumptions explicitly demonstrates clarity of thought and invites the interviewer to correct you before you waste time. Common assumptions include eventual consistency being acceptable, read-heavy traffic patterns, and users being globally distributed.

data.title: Assumption Statement Example
data.content: I assume that the system is read-heavy with a 95:5 read-to-write ratio. I also assume eventual consistency is acceptable for user profiles, meaning updated data may take up to a few seconds to propagate globally. Please correct me if these assumptions are wrong.

terms.definition: The uncontrolled expansion of project requirements beyond the originally agreed boundaries.
A limiting factor that shapes design decisions, such as budget, timeline, or technology restrictions.
A statement taken to be true without proof, used to simplify the problem space in system design.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Identify constraints early to avoid dead-end solutions
State assumptions out loud in interviews
Revisit scope when the interviewer introduces new requirements
data.takeaway: Clear scope and well-documented constraints turn a vague interview question into a structured, solvable design problem.
